newsitem.title: MONTSERRAT: Montserrat volcano belches more ash, lava.
newsitem.headline: Montserrat volcano belches more ash, lava.

text.p: The Soufriere Hills volcano belched ash sporadically on Tuesday and two new flows snaked down its sides, Montserrat officials said.
But no new damage was reported on the Caribbean island, suffering from its worst volcanic activity since devastating eruptions in 1995.
The official death toll stood at nine, with 24 people missing, government spokesman Howard Sergeant said. Officials said Monday they feared the final toll could reach 20 people.
Sergeant said there were two new pyroclastic flows -- fast-moving bursts of 930-degree Fahrenheit (500-degree Celsius) volcanic material -- on Tuesday morning.
"One went down the east side and one went down the southwest. It was heading in the direction of Plymouth (the capital) but stopped before it got there," he said.
The volcano was spewing ash at intervals of several hours, Sergeant added.
Flows devastated seven villages in southern Montserrat last week. More than 1,000 people have been evacuated and at last 200 homes have been destroyed.
Caribbean leaders meeting in Montego Bay, Jamaica, pledged to support Montserrat but said colonial ruler Britain must shoulder most of the responsibility.
Montserrat's chief minister Bertrand Osbourne is not attending the Caribbean Community (Caricom) summit because of the disaster.
At Monday's night's opening ceremony, Antiguan prime minister Lester Bird said his country, Montserrat's closest neighbour, "will continue to open its doors to Montserratians" and give them shelter.

The summit will attempt to coordinate medical teams, supplies and other aid. Bird said, however, that any aid must be provided "primarily by the government of the United Kingdom, whose responsibility Montserrat remains."
In London, a member of parliament blamed many of the deaths caused by the volcanic eruption last week on poor resettlement efforts after the previous eruption.
Labor legislator Diane Abbott said small farmers who left the volcano area two years ago had come back to their land in the danger zone "because that was the only way they felt they could survive."

"Had there been proper housing, had there been proper arrangements made for their resettlement, they would not have lost their lives," Abbott said. Government ministers did not directly comment on Abbott's claims.

Baroness Liz Symons, British undersecretary of state with responsibility for the Caribbean, visited Montserrat this week and reiterated her government's commitment to giving financial support to the tiny island and to developing its northern third, which is considered safe.
The population of Montserrat, which relies on tourism and rice-growing, fell to about 6,800 from 11,000 when the volcano first became active.
Last week's deaths were the first blamed on the volcano since it roared to life on July 18, 1995, after nearly four centuries of virtual dormancy.
